channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You judge your behavior by your circumstances, not character.
item.description: Jones and Nisbett (1971) proposed the actor-observer asymmetry hypothesis, though subsequent meta-analyses have found little evidence that this behavior is a reliable or consistent psychological phenomenon.

item.title: A third option changes what you choose entirely.
item.description: A 1982 study found that adding a clearly inferior third option increases the likelihood that people will choose the original preferred option.

item.title: You become less careful when you feel safer.
item.description: Peltzman's 1975 study argued that mandatory automobile safety regulations did not lead to the predicted decrease in aggregate traffic fatality rates because drivers engaged in offsetting risky behavior.

item.title: New experiences make time feel like it's slowing.
item.description: Initial studies suggested an unexpected stimulus makes its duration appear 30–50% longer, though later research shows the effect is generally around 10% or less.

item.title: You assume attractive people are also morally good.
item.description: While Thorndike identified the 'halo effect' as a general cognitive error in 1920, the systematic experimental finding that physical attractiveness correlates with perceived intelligence and morality was established later.

item.title: You rewrite your history to appear prescient.
item.description: A 1975 study revealed that after an event occurred, participants significantly overestimated how likely they were to have predicted it beforehand.

item.title: You consistently underestimate the time tasks will take.
item.description: A 1994 study found that students predicted they would finish their thesis projects in 33 days, but actually took an average of 55 days.

item.title: You work faster as the finish line appears.
item.description: A 2006 study by Kivetz, Urminsky, and Zheng provided empirical evidence supporting the goal gradient effect in consumer loyalty programs.

item.title: You confuse high physiological arousal for romantic attraction.
item.description: The brain often misinterprets physical adrenaline or fear as feelings of attraction toward a person nearby.

item.title: You judge people's actions based on their internal character.
item.description: People tend to attribute others' behavior to character while attributing their own behavior to circumstances, a phenomenon known as the actor-observer bias.

item.title: You work less hard when you think you are in a team.
item.description: While Ringelmann's 1913 study observed that group output is less than the sum of individual efforts, he attributed this primarily to coordination failures ('lack of simultaneity') rather than the psychological motivation loss known as 'social loafing'.

item.title: You eventually believe a claim you once knew was false.
item.description: Over time, the source of a message is forgotten, but the information it contained persists in your memory.

item.title: You forget the negative emotions of past events faster.
item.description: The emotional intensity associated with negative memories fades more rapidly than the intensity of positive memories.

item.title: You feel a frantic need to move during static crises.
item.description: The 2007 study by Bar-Eli et al. demonstrates that goalkeepers choose to jump to the side even though staying in the center is statistically more likely to result in a save.

item.title: You assume your future self will share your current desires.
item.description: The 2003 paper by Loewenstein, O'Donoghue, and Rabin established the theoretical framework for 'projection bias' that explains why people fail to predict changes in preferences.

item.title: You think your inner state is visible to everyone.
item.description: The 'illusion of transparency' is a verified psychological phenomenon where individuals overestimate the extent to which their internal states are visible to others.

item.title: You are physically unable to forget what you already know.
item.description: Once you learn a piece of information, you consistently overestimate others' ability to guess it.

item.title: Your memory of an event ignores most of its duration.
item.description: The peak intensity and the final moments of an experience define your entire retrospective evaluation.

item.title: You rate people as smarter based on their role.
item.description: A 1977 study found that participants rated 'questioners' in a quiz show as more intelligent than 'contestants'.

item.title: You perform better around others on simple tasks.
item.description: A 1965 study demonstrated that the mere presence of others increases the likelihood of your dominant response.

item.title: You become more likeable when you commit a blunder.
item.description: A 1966 study found that a highly competent person is perceived as more likeable after making a clumsy mistake.

item.title: You are a member of a group just by existing.
item.description: A 1970 study showed that people favored others simply because they were assigned to the same arbitrary group, even when the groups had no meaning.

item.title: You want to believe the world is inherently fair.
item.description: A 1966 study by Lerner and Simmons found that observers are more likely to disparage an innocent victim when they feel unable to intervene or compensate the victim for their suffering.

item.title: You treat people based on your expectations of them.
item.description: A 1968 study found that when teachers were told certain students were academic 'bloomers,' those students showed significantly higher IQ gains by the end of the year.

item.title: You adapt your behavior to fit what others expect.
item.description: A 1974 study found that high self-monitors consistently changed their behavior to match the social situation, whereas low self-monitors acted consistently regardless of the setting.

item.title: You feel more capable when you believe you have control.
item.description: A 1975 study demonstrated that people were less likely to sell a lottery ticket if they were the ones who had chosen the numbers personally.

item.title: You like the things you choose more than you did.
item.description: A 1956 study found that after being asked to rate several household appliances, participants rated the one they chose to keep as significantly more attractive than the one they rejected.

item.title: You only cheat when you can justify it to yourself.
item.description: A 2008 study found that participants were less likely to cheat when asked to recall the Ten Commandments, but cheated frequently when given subtle prompts to redefine their actions.

item.title: You value things more simply because you own them.
item.description: A 1990 study found that participants required nearly twice as much money to part with a mug they owned (willingness to accept) as they were willing to pay to acquire the same mug in the first place (willingness to pay).

item.title: You only notice your own effort in group work.
item.description: When people are asked to estimate their contribution to a shared task, the sum of their estimates consistently exceeds 100%.

item.title: Your self-control is exhausted by simple mental math.
item.description: In a 1999 study, participants who were asked to memorize a seven-digit number were about 1.5 times more likely to choose chocolate cake over fruit salad than those who memorized a two-digit number.

item.title: You accept vague personality descriptions as deeply personal.
item.description: Participants in a 1948 study rated a generic, personality-neutral paragraph as highly accurate when told it was written specifically for them.

item.title: You feel a frantic urge to act during uncertainty.
item.description: In a study of professional soccer penalty kicks, goalkeepers were statistically more likely to dive left or right than to stay in the center, despite staying still yielding better outcomes.

item.title: You think others are more similar than they are.
item.description: Individuals consistently perceive members of their own group as highly diverse, while viewing outsiders as a uniform, homogenous group.

item.title: You believe you control events that are entirely random.
item.description: A 1975 study showed that people overestimate their chances of winning a game of pure luck if they have performed a personal ritual, like choosing their own lottery ticket.

item.title: Your mood acts as a filter for your memory.
item.description: People are significantly more likely to recall memories that match their current emotional state than those that do not.

item.title: You are biologically tuned to catch social cheaters.
item.description: People consistently fail abstract logic puzzles but solve identical problems easily when they involve detecting rule-breakers in a social context.

item.title: You only remember the beginning and the end.
item.description: Ebbinghaus (1885) identified the serial position effect, but the explanation attributing it to the interaction between short-term working memory and long-term memory is a modern interpretation.

item.title: You are more motivated on the first of January.
item.description: A 2014 study found that people seek more 'fresh start' opportunities during temporal landmarks like birthdays or new years.

item.title: You are blind to changes happening right before you.
item.description: In a 1998 study, about half of the participants failed to notice when the person they were talking to was swapped for another.

item.title: The default choice shapes your entire life's direction.
item.description: While researchers like Johnson and Goldstein have shown that default settings correlate with higher registration rates, the actual number of transplants is strongly influenced by healthcare infrastructure, public trust, and logistical coordination, rather than being solely driven by the opt-out default.

item.title: You seek out people who confirm your negative traits.
item.description: A 1983 study showed that people preferred feedback that aligned with their existing self-conception.

item.title: Anxiety about performance can lower your actual results.
item.description: A 1995 study found that black students performed worse on tests when reminded of negative stereotypes about their intelligence.

item.title: Telling you not to do it makes it attractive.
item.description: A 1977 study by Brehm and Weinraub found that restricting access to a toy increased its desirability to children.

item.title: Your brain is outsourcing your memory to technology.
item.description: A 2011 study found that people are less likely to remember facts if they believe they can search them later.

item.title: You assume everyone shares your private opinions.
item.description: A 1977 study showed that people who agreed to wear a sandwich board were more likely to believe others would too.

item.title: You prefer things simply because you see them often.
item.description: A 1968 study showed that participants rated symbols they had viewed more frequently as having a more positive meaning.

item.title: A random number drastically alters your next choice.
item.description: In a 1974 study, spinning a wheel of fortune influenced participants' subsequent estimates of geographical data.

item.title: You believe you are safer than the average person.
item.description: A 1980 study found that most adults rate their personal risk of accidents as significantly lower than their peers.

item.title: You understand your own car less than you think.
item.description: Participants in a 2002 study overestimated their ability to explain how zippers and toilets work.
